newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Japan to snap up U.S. corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Japan to snap up U.S. corn.

text.p: South Korean and Japanese buyers will probably buy U.S. corn after recent price falls in Chicago and ahead of a steady rise in trans-Pacific freight rates to the end of the year, regional traders said on Monday.
Korean feedmakers will likely move into the corn market this week after the December contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) fell 2-3/4 U.S. cents to end on Friday at US$2.75-1/4 a bushel.
Korean grain traders had said buyers were waiting for prices to fall below $2.80 a bushel before jumping into the market.

"We think $2.70 a bushel will be the bottom of the current trend. Some will move to buy and to cover their corn needs for mid-next year (1997) shipment when that price is reached," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.
But some traders at Seoul-based foreign grain export companies said local buyers showed some reluctance to buy corn even though prices had already broken the $2.80 a bushel level.

"They are not likely to buy at current levels until prices appear to fully bottom (out) since they seemed to regret their hasty purchases at the highest price level (a few) months ago," said a trader at a Seoul-based Japanese grain trading house.
"Our clients have already changed their target prices to $2.65 (a bushel) from $2.80 a week ago. They seem to change their target prices every day," the trader said.
South Korean flour millers are also expected to buy one or two cargoes of U.S. wheat for January to February shipment this week, dealers said.
"There may be some wheat buyers who will cover their January shipment needs. It will be one or two cargoes," said a wheat trader of a leading flour milling firm.
In Japan, grain traders said they will continue to buy U.S. corn this week ahead of a possible increase in trans-Pacific freight rates.
Japanese importers have bought about 80 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn, with premiums at 97 to 98 U.S. cents a bushel on the CBOT March futures contract, the traders said.
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route were quoted currently at about US$23 a tonne.
"We'll continue to buy U.S. corn this week ahead of further freight rises," a major trade house official said.
The likelihood of increasing freight rates, rather than price falls in the Chicago corn market, is motivating Japanese importers to cover their U.S. grain needs, he said.

The traders also expressed their concern about the inspection system of American grain exporters, pointing out that recently arrived shipments of U.S. corn were found to have mould because of higher-than-usual moisture.

"U.S. exporters failed to dry corn completely when they shipped to Japan, and some U.S. corn cargoes were covered with mould. We're going to request U.S. exporters to settle the problem," another trade house official said.
Japanese importers are currently buying U.S. soybean for December shipment with premiums at 125 to 126 U.S. cents a bushel on the CBOT January futures contract, the traders said.
A Chinese grain mission is now visiting Japan to discuss export contracts for the first half of calendar 1997 with Japanese buyers.
"Negotiations are going on now. I can't tell if we can reach any deal at the moment," a soybean trader said.
The mission includes officials from the Chinese grain agency Cereals Oils and Feedstuffs Import and Export Corp and Heilongjiang province, which grows most of China's soybeans.
Chinese soybeans are mainly used for making miso, or bean paste, in Japan.

Taiwan may also tender for 70,000 tonnes of corn and 38,000 tonnes of soybeans this week while Manila will hold a tender on Tuesday for 150,000 tonnes of corn and look into buying up to 35,000 tonnes of wheat, traders in both countries said.
